title: Persian GPT — Transformer From Scratch
description: Public from-scratch Persian language-model artifact. A pinned metadata-only check counted 134,994,432 stored tensor elements in the exported safetensors file; the model card states a 110.4M architecture. Runtime tying and the reported evaluation have not been independently reproduced.
type: Flagship model · Persian NLP · From-scratch training
note: Independent safetensors-header count of published checkpoint, not an independently reproduced training or performance result.

research.context: This project demonstrates an end-to-end low-resource language-model workflow for Persian, from corpus preparation through tokenizer design, training, and held-out evaluation.
methods: 855,724 cleaned Persian Wikipedia documents
Custom 32K byte-pair encoding tokenizer
PyTorch decoder-only Transformer
N-gram baselines and held-out perplexity
research.limitations: Public safetensors revision b443d45edab7a464edb25f49d0c4b44f05f4a739 stores 134,994,432 tensor elements (149 tensors, all F16), including an explicit 24,576,000-element lm_head.weight. The 110.4M claimed architecture count is therefore different from the file's stored count. Runtime weight sharing, training and perplexity 14.52 remain unverified.

caseStudy.title: Persian GPT from scratch: a Persian language model
caseStudy.description: A Persian language-modeling experiment using a 32K BPE tokenizer, PyTorch and author-reported held-out perplexity. A pinned header-only check counted 134,994,432 stored tensor elements in the public safetensors checkpoint.
caseStudy.lede: An end-to-end Persian language-modeling experiment, from preparing a cleaned Wikipedia corpus and building a tokenizer to training a decoder-only Transformer and comparing held-out perplexity against n-gram baselines.
caseStudy.challenge: Persian has fewer openly documented from-scratch training examples than high-resource languages. The goal here was to build a transparent, reproducible baseline workflow and document what the resulting language-model metric does and does not establish.
approach: Cleaned and prepared 855,724 Persian Wikipedia documents, totaling about 244 million training tokens.
Trained a custom 32,000-token byte-pair encoding tokenizer on the prepared corpus.

The model card describes a 12-layer decoder-only Transformer trained in PyTorch for two epochs; a separate public safetensors-header audit found 134,994,432 stored tensor elements versus the card's intended 110.4M design.
Evaluated the held-out split with loss and perplexity, then compared perplexity with unigram and interpolated 5-gram baselines.
results: Held-out test perplexity: 14.52; validation perplexity: 14.02.
The held-out interpolated 5-gram baseline perplexity was 171.60, and the unigram baseline was 1,590.26.

At published revision b443d45edab7a464edb25f49d0c4b44f05f4a739, the public checkpoint stores 134,994,432 tensor elements, independently enumerated from its safetensors header; this does not resolve runtime tying.
caseStudy.limitations: This small research portfolio model is trained on Wikipedia rather than a broad conversational distribution. The independently inspected file stores 134,994,432 tensor elements; the model card states 110.4M, and the output head is explicitly stored. Weight equality and runtime tying have NOT been checked, and the author-reported perplexity 14.52 is not independently reproduced. No factuality, safety or downstream usefulness has been established.

title: 3D Cardiac MRI Segmentation
description: A research-oriented 3D left-atrium segmentation experiment using PyTorch, MONAI, and a two-class U-Net. It documents NIfTI loading, case-level splitting, mixed-precision training, sliding-window inference and an author-reported MSD Task02 Heart validation metric.
note: Research project on a public benchmark dataset; best validation Dice of 0.8821 is author-reported, exact split/reproduction not independently established, and no clinical validation.

research.context: The documented model predicts left atrium versus background in volumetric cardiac MRI. Split independence and external validation must be established before interpreting the score as a comparative scientific benchmark.
methods: MSD Task02 Heart; NIfTI images and corresponding left-atrium labels
Filename-matched case-level randomized split: 16 train, remaining validation, seed 42
PyTorch/MONAI two-class 3D U-Net with DiceCELoss and AdamW
Mixed-precision training, patch sampling and sliding-window inference
research.limitations: The 0.8821 validation Dice is author-reported; dataset split provenance, checkpoint and independent evaluation remain unverified. No external clinical validation is claimed.

caseStudy.title: 3D cardiac MRI segmentation with MONAI and a 3D U-Net
caseStudy.description: A two-class background/left-atrium cardiac MRI segmentation experiment built with PyTorch, MONAI, MSD Task02 Heart data, a 3D U-Net and sliding-window inference.
caseStudy.lede: A documented research workflow for segmenting the left atrium in cardiac MRI. The code covers NIfTI loading, case splitting, volumetric preprocessing, 3D U-Net training, sliding-window inference and author-reported validation Dice.
caseStudy.challenge: The goal is left-atrium segmentation in 3D cardiac MRI volumes, where spatial context, image/label alignment, split provenance and reliable validation matter. The current case-level split is reproducible in code, but patient-level group independence has not been independently demonstrated.
approach: Used the MSD Task02 Heart dataset, with expected matching NIfTI image and left-atrium label filenames.
Shuffled image/label pairs deterministically with seed 42, taking 16 for training and the remainder for validation.
Defined a MONAI/PyTorch 3D U-Net with two output classes, AdamW and DiceCELoss; nominal 100 epochs.
Used patch-based training and sliding-window validation inference; the original checkpoint and independent reproduction are not included.
results: Best author-reported validation Dice: 0.8821; the exact validation split and reproduction artifacts are not established in the public README.
Training configuration: 100 epochs, 3D U-Net, mixed-precision training.
The figure and 0.8821 Dice are author-provided; this is not a patient-level audited split, third-party benchmark, external-site result, or clinical performance estimate.
caseStudy.limitations: This work has not been clinically validated, prospectively tested or evaluated across external institutions and scanner settings. It is not a diagnostic device or clinical decision-support system. The author-reported validation result cannot be independently reproduced from the currently described split and run artifacts.

caseStudy.title: Multi-agent AI research assistant with LangGraph and RAG
caseStudy.description: A multi-agent research assistant using LangGraph, ChromaDB RAG, FastAPI, parallel research, cited synthesis, persistent state, and offline tests.
caseStudy.lede: A full-stack research workflow that combines planning, retrieval, parallel research, tool execution, cited synthesis, bounded reflection, persistent state, and server-sent event streaming.
caseStudy.challenge: Research tasks often require several different operations: break down a query, retrieve relevant material, gather evidence, synthesize findings, and preserve progress. This project explores how to orchestrate those steps in a testable, stateful application.
approach: Used LangGraph to coordinate five roles and parallel research branches.
Connected ChromaDB retrieval with local ONNX embeddings and configurable research tools.
Implemented FastAPI REST and server-sent event (SSE) interfaces, with SQLite checkpointing for persistent workflow state.
Added citation-grounded synthesis, bounded reflection, LangSmith evaluation tooling, and deterministic offline tests.
results: The repository reports 103 offline tests for application behavior in deterministic fake-LLM mode.
The workflow exposes REST and SSE interfaces and includes five agent roles.
Tests exercise software contracts; they are not a measure of answer correctness, evidence quality, or research usefulness.
caseStudy.limitations: The deterministic fake-LLM test mode validates application behavior rather than live-model answer quality. The system has not been shown to outperform human research workflows or establish the correctness and completeness of generated research. Human verification of cited sources remains necessary.

title: PsyLex Studio — English–Persian Psychology Translator
description: A local-first Windows desktop application for psychology terminology and English-to-Iranian-Persian translation. Built with Python and PySide6, it combines an offline bilingual dictionary, user-imported DOCX terminology, optional Ollama/LM Studio or cloud LLMs, OCR, document review, secure API-key storage, and a packaged Windows installer.
note: Public edition includes a 16-term original starter glossary. Users import their own authorized dictionaries; the two reference books and their extracted lexicon are not redistributed. AI output and OCR require human verification.

research.context: Psychology translation requires careful handling of established terminology, research statistics, and contextual differences between English and Iranian Persian. PsyLex is a working desktop software project, not a claim of evaluated model superiority.
methods: PySide6 Windows application with offline SQLite dictionary and terminology evidence
Optional local inference through running Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp, or vLLM servers; cloud APIs including OpenRouter
RapidOCR-based local recognition plus optional cloud OCR adapters and document review workflow
OS-backed provider credentials, first-launch model discovery, Windows PyInstaller/Inno Setup distribution
research.limitations: The public edition has only a 16-term sample glossary rather than a comprehensive psychology dictionary. Model servers and cloud services are external dependencies. Recognition and generated translations need human review. It is not a clinical assessment or decision-support system.

caseStudy.title: PsyLex Studio: a local-first psychology translation workbench
caseStudy.description: PsyLex Studio is a PySide6 Windows application combining English-to-Persian psychology terminology search, optional local/cloud LLM translation, OCR, editable document workflows, and a downloadable installer.
caseStudy.lede: An installable bilingual psychology desktop workbench: search local terminology, connect an optional language model, extract scanned documents, review Persian results, and export work—all with a clear boundary between the open-source app and privately imported dictionaries.
caseStudy.challenge: General-purpose translation can miss domain-specific psychology vocabulary, distort statistical statements, or ignore whether a phrase is a verified term or generated text. This project focuses on a usable English-to-Iranian-Persian workflow that keeps local reference evidence distinct from LLM output and offers a practical Windows release.
approach: Developed a Python/PySide6 desktop UI with Dictionary, Translation, Documents, Batch, History, Favorites, and Dictionary & Data workspaces.
Implemented SQLite-backed glossary search and DOCX terminology imports, keeping user-imported data local and avoiding redistribution of third-party reference books.
Connected optional local inference servers (Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp, vLLM) and supported online providers, with first-launch discovery and Windows Credential Manager-backed API keys.
Added RapidOCR-based recognition, optional OCR provider integrations, segment-by-segment editing, export, and review signals for psychology terminology.
Built Windows packaging using PyInstaller and Inno Setup, with Python regression tests, GUI smoke tests, and a packaged executable self-test.
results: PsyLex Studio v0.6.5 source code and a downloadable Windows installer are published on GitHub Releases.
The available OCR catalog includes two local options and six online adapters; local model discovery supports four running server families.
The public-source edition ships a 16-term original starter glossary and can import user-authorized bilingual DOCX terminology.
caseStudy.limitations: This is applied desktop software, not a validated clinical translation system or a benchmark showing improved translation accuracy. The sample glossary is intentionally limited; local models require separate runtimes, cloud services may charge, and OCR/LLM output needs expert review. Dependency redistribution licenses are handled separately from the MIT license for original code.

title: From Messy Data to Meaningful Insight — Psychology Research Atlas
description: A bilingual, interactive data-science case study: I audited 240 psychological questionnaire records, discovered only 86 distinct answer patterns, and showed how an apparent group difference nearly vanishes when the original item answers are checked.
type: Applied data science · Psychology · Data integrity
note: The interactive page prioritizes clear insight storytelling; the complete bilingual reports and R script are available as downloads. The raw participant responses are withheld.

research.context: A public-friendly story about moving from seemingly straightforward group statistics to responsible insight by checking the underlying SPSS data and score construction.
methods: Audited 240 rows and 89 original variables
Identified 86 distinct response patterns and matching cross-group answers
Compared stored scale totals with direct item-sum diagnostics
Communicated findings through bilingual interactive explanation and full report downloads
research.limitations: Exploratory audit, not a validated between-group effect. Original group meaning, source integrity, and official questionnaire scoring rules remain unverified. Participant-level raw.sav is not public.

caseStudy.title: From messy psychology data to meaningful, defensible insight
caseStudy.seoTitle: From Messy Data to Meaningful Insight | Psychology Research Atlas
caseStudy.description: An interactive bilingual case study demonstrating data cleaning, data-integrity investigation, and responsible statistical storytelling for psychology questionnaire data.
caseStudy.lede: How checking questionnaire response patterns changed a seemingly obvious group comparison and made the real finding understandable.
caseStudy.challenge: Stored scores appeared to show a group difference, but repeated response patterns and uncertain scoring threatened the validity of that claim.
approach: Examined response patterns and score construction before interpreting results.
Compared stored ambiguity totals against direct sums of item answers.
Explained the evidence, its limitations, and the practical takeaway in English and Persian.
results: 240 recorded rows but 86 distinct 76-item answer patterns.
119 of 120 aligned cross-group record pairs have matching item responses.
The stored ambiguity-score gap of approximately 4.63 contrasts with a direct item-sum gap of only 0.08; neither comparison establishes a validated independent-group effect.
caseStudy.limitations: Direct item sums are diagnostic and not official validated scores; study design, independence, and scoring keys remain unverified. Complete reports and an untested R source script are downloadable; individual raw responses are withheld.

title: Holdout Ledger: Dataset Leakage Audit Workbench
description: A local workbench for inspecting text and entity overlap across train, validation, and test splits. Includes an evidence dashboard, offline reports, SQLite audit snapshots, and reviewed repair plans that preserve every test record. CI checks track newly exposed holdout IDs; lexical detection limits are documented.
note: Local synthetic demonstration and hosted CI do not establish detection performance on naturally occurring datasets; third-party adoption is not verified.

research.context: Unrecognized overlap between training and holdout records can undermine evaluation, even when explicit record identifiers are unique. This project is a text and declared-entity-group audit workbench, not a medical image similarity tool.
methods: Normalized-exact text witnesses and verified lexical near-copy matches
Declared group IDs for known subjects, sessions, or document families
Connected-component evidence, offline HTML review, and SQLite audit history
Source-fingerprint-bound review plans and separate repaired outputs that preserve held-out test records
Seeded synthetic regression and same-input baseline checks on GitHub Actions
research.limitations: Only text and declared entity group boundaries are checked. It cannot discover unknown participant identity, semantic paraphrases, hidden data provenance, or prove that an evaluation is leakage-free. Benchmark control outcomes do not generalize to naturally occurring datasets. No external user adoption or independent study validation is verified.

caseStudy.title: Holdout Ledger: inspect train/test overlap with reviewable evidence
caseStudy.description: A local MIT-licensed Python workbench for normalized-exact, lexical near-copy and declared entity-group split audits with source-bound repair plans and a self-contained synthetic demo.
caseStudy.lede: Data leakage can conceal itself behind apparently distinct record IDs. Holdout Ledger lets an engineer open a small local example, inspect the witnesses behind cross-split matches, review a proposed repair, and save a separate provenance-bearing result.
caseStudy.challenge: An aggregate duplicate count does not explain which exact records cross the evaluation boundary, how near-copies or groups connect, or whether a repair safely preserves held-out examples.
approach: Builds bounded, explainable normalized-exact and lexical near-copy evidence, along with group-ID overlap checks.
Represents connected components with source-split membership and individual match witnesses.
Provides local CLI, a FastAPI-backed evidence explorer, offline HTML reports, and persisted SQLite audits.
Generates source-fingerprint-bound plans that require human review, preserve test records, and write repaired data separately.
Runs seeded synthetic controls and reproducibility-related CI checks; feedback is voluntary and must not include patient or proprietary data.
results: The documented invented-records demo runs locally without a GPU, remote model API, account, or dataset download.
GitHub Actions passed on the main branch on 2026-10-16; this verifies the configured checks, not field performance.
Public onboarding includes a first-run walkthrough and optional privacy-safe tester feedback form.
caseStudy.limitations: Detection is restricted to normalized-exact text, lexical near matches, and declared entity groups. A cluster may be transitive; pairs within it need not directly match. Semantic paraphrases, missing group identity, unseen sources, and real-world leakage can escape the audit. No independent real-world sensitivity, clinical utility, or user-adoption figures are established.

title: Emotion & Appraisal Repeated-Measures Analysis
description: 13,264 recorded observations map to 434 worker IDs and 3,316 HITs. Explore why row counts, quality criteria, and worker-level inference must be distinguished.

caseStudy.title: Emotion & Appraisal Repeated-Measures Analysis
caseStudy.description: 13,264 recorded observations map to 434 worker IDs and 3,316 HITs. Explore why row counts, quality criteria, and worker-level inference must be distinguished.
caseStudy.lede: The dataset appeared ready for a quick emotional-intensity analysis. Instead, I audited its row structure, quality flags, durations, and scoring formulas before interpreting any association.
caseStudy.challenge: Two quality flags tell very different stories. That does not automatically mean either is incorrect; they may implement distinct criteria. The difference is a prompt to audit the definitions.
results: 13,264 rows arise from 434 worker IDs, with four entries per HIT.
Only 4 rows fail QUALITY_CRITERION, while 1,226 fail ALL_CRITERIA.
The worker-aggregated Spearman rho is +0.035 (n=432), while a singular worker-intercept model returns -2.377, a numerically unstable estimate requiring caution.
24 rows have dur_in_sec above 24 hours; the recorded maximum is 312.24 hours.
caseStudy.limitations: The mixed model accounts for worker intercepts, not crossed HIT or video dependence. Neither the row-level nor worker-level result demonstrates causation.
approach: Audited worker IDs, HITs, and four observations per HIT before choosing a statistical unit.
Compared QUALITY_CRITERION and ALL_CRITERIA flags and inspected recorded duration extremes without dropping observations.
Compared worker-aggregated associations, a worker-intercept mixed model, and worker-cluster-robust estimates while disclosing singular-fit limitations.

title: Digital Survey Response Quality Analysis
description: The survey export contains 0 literal CSV-null cells but 395,994 negative-coded numeric entries and 14,793 blank-string cells. Inspect the recorded codes and their limits.

caseStudy.title: Digital Survey Response Quality Analysis
caseStudy.description: The survey export contains 0 literal CSV-null cells but 395,994 negative-coded numeric entries and 14,793 blank-string cells. Inspect the recorded codes and their limits.
caseStudy.lede: There are 4,771 unique case numbers and 289 fields. Literal-null checks alone would call the export complete, but its negative codes and blank strings tell a more complicated story.
caseStudy.challenge: The visible comparison switches between CSV-null cells and negative-coded numeric entries. The latter are observed codes, not assumed missingness, until the original instrument defines them.
results: The table has no literal CSV null cells, while 395,994 numeric cells carry one of the observed negative codes.
RQI_breakoff is 1 for 713 records, the same number as cases whose status differs from 6.
710 Extraversion_mean entries are blank strings even though the CSV has zero nulls.
The reported device-code group comparison needs a codebook to interpret groups 0 and 1 correctly.
caseStudy.limitations: The exact meanings of -1, -2, -3, -5, -96, -97, and -98 are not supplied. The published sample frame, raking calibration and codebook need verification.
approach: Inspected all 289 fields across 4,771 cases without silently interpreting negative response codes as missing data.
Compared literal CSV nulls, blank-string entries, negative-coded cells, and RQI_breakoff flags.
Marked coded values and device labels as unresolved pending codebook and sampling-weight verification; reported exploratory group comparisons only.

title: Psoriasis & Wellbeing Survey Analysis
description: In a published 722-record psoriasis survey, no CSV-null cells appear, but 50 values are coded -9 across 20 records. Explore the effect of coded responses and scoring assumptions.

caseStudy.title: Psoriasis & Wellbeing Survey Analysis
caseStudy.description: In a published 722-record psoriasis survey, no CSV-null cells appear, but 50 values are coded -9 across 20 records. Explore the effect of coded responses and scoring assumptions.
caseStudy.lede: The 36-field file is semicolon-delimited with comma decimals. Without parsing it correctly and inspecting -9 response codes, a simple spreadsheet analysis could misrepresent missingness.
caseStudy.challenge: The interactive reveal contrasts zero literal CSV nulls with 50 observed -9 cells. The values remain unchanged; only a separately labeled sensitivity check treats -9 as unavailable.
results: 722 records and 36 variables parse correctly only with semicolon delimiters; comma decimals require a separate option.
The file contains zero literal nulls but 50 -9 cells spread across 20 records.
The raw-direction 12-item HA03 coefficient alpha is 0.248 for 711 complete cases under a -9-unavailable sensitivity assumption.
Age spans 12 to 85 and a raw HA03 item mean differs modestly across an explicitly chosen age-40 split.
caseStudy.limitations: Published as Schuster et al. (2021), PsychArchives CC BY 4.0, DOI 10.23668/psycharchives.4451. Only aggregate derivatives are included in this local review ZIP.
approach: Parsed semicolon-separated records and decimal commas; checked 722 rows and 36 fields against the source format.
Counted literal null cells separately from recorded -9 values, leaving the original responses unchanged.
Computed explicitly qualified -9-unavailable sensitivity results and raw-direction reliability diagnostics without claiming validated clinical scores.

caseStudy.title: MindHealth Observatory: Depression screening, population inequality and survey-weighted inference
caseStudy.seoTitle: MindHealth Observatory | R Statistical Research | Arad
caseStudy.description: Depression screening, population inequality and survey-weighted inference. Review the planned estimands, R methods, source data and scientific limits. Partial real-data R execution is documented; independent validation remains pending.
caseStudy.lede: An open, statistics-first investigation of CDC NHANES 2017–2018. Explore the question, planned analysis, sample-design requirements and limitations, with explicitly preliminary real-data execution evidence.
caseStudy.challenge: How does the prevalence of elevated depressive symptoms differ across socioeconomic and demographic strata once the NHANES sample design is respected?
approach: Validate all nine PHQ-9 symptoms and survey eligibility before scoring.
Use 2-year MEC weights, masked strata and PSU identifiers for design-based estimates.
Estimate weighted prevalence, survey-weighted GLMs, design-aware confidence intervals and nonlinear income sensitivity.
Audit complete-case selection and report all weights, denominators and exclusion rules.
results: An R 4.5.0 execution on CDC NHANES 2017–2018 analyzed 5,068 eligible complete PHQ-9 respondents. Design-weighted PHQ-9 ≥10 prevalence was 8.53% (95% CI 7.52%–9.55%; SE 0.52 percentage points). This is a screening threshold, not a clinical diagnosis.
The observed execution artifacts, input hashes, package versions and restrictions are documented in the research evidence ledger. Full reproducibility and sensitivity gates are still outstanding.
Interpretation remains exploratory and no causal, diagnostic or peer-reviewed conclusion is asserted.

Fresh design-based sensitivity on the same 5,068 respondents found PHQ-9 screen-positive percentages of 24.72% (cutoff 5), 8.53% (cutoff 10), and 2.81% (cutoff 15). These are descriptive screening cutoffs, not diagnoses.
caseStudy.limitations: The reported estimate and SE were obtained from an observed R run, but have not been independently replicated; NHANES nonresponse, single-cycle design and complete-item exclusion constrain generalization.

Assess sparse pairwise overlap before estimating polychoric correlations.

caseStudy.title: Psychemetrics Atlas: Latent dimensions, item coverage and the limits of personality measurement
caseStudy.seoTitle: Psychemetrics Atlas | R Statistical Research | Arad
caseStudy.description: Latent dimensions, item coverage and the limits of personality measurement. Review the planned estimands, R methods, source data and scientific limits. Partial real-data R execution is documented; independent validation remains pending.
caseStudy.lede: An open, statistics-first investigation of SAPA public personality questionnaires. Explore the question, planned analysis, sample-design requirements and limitations, with explicitly preliminary real-data execution evidence.
caseStudy.challenge: How stable are exploratory personality item dimensions when respondents encounter only subsets of a large questionnaire?
approach: Audit item codebooks, scales, reverse-coding and response coverage.
Assess sparse pairwise overlap before estimating polychoric correlations.
Explore oblique factor solutions, eigenstructure and item-level sensitivity.
Separate unkeyed descriptive scale consistency from validated trait reliability.
Audit all five 10-item IPIP-50 signed keys, original item-text mappings, reverse coding, completeness thresholds, and pairwise coadministration before trait-scale inference.
results: Original Harvard Dataverse SAPA RData contained 23,679 respondent rows. Five ten-item signed IPIP-50 keys were checked against original item descriptions and response categories. In every scale, ZERO respondents supplied all ten responses, making conventional complete-case full-scale reliability inappropriate.

With at least five of ten items answered, counts ranged from 307 to 535 per selected scale. Minimum pairwise item overlap per scale ranged from 289 to 523. Positive keyed pair correlations are exploratory association evidence—not a substitute for full-scale reliability, measurement invariance, or validity.

The earlier IRW item-table transformation contains 23,678 respondent IDs and 2,039,803 observed item responses, with exploratory three-factor EFA of 12 high-coverage items. Source representations and their one-record count discrepancy have not been reconciled respondent by respondent.
caseStudy.limitations: Nonprobability volunteer sampling and extreme planned item missingness: no complete 10-item records in the selected IPIP-50 scales. Pairwise correlations are descriptive; no ordinary complete-case alpha, validated factor scores, invariance, or clinical conclusions. One-row discrepancy remains between original RData and the separate IRW transformation. Independent publication-level reproducibility is pending.

caseStudy.description: PISA 2022 survey-weighted analysis of the published BELONG index for 78 economies, using Fay-BRR variance and explicit data exclusions. Preliminary findings only.
caseStudy.lede: A statistical investigation of PISA 2022 school belonging. The actual 2.1 GB student file was processed in memory-bounded batches, and valid survey-weighted estimates and confidence intervals were obtained for 78 economies.
caseStudy.challenge: Do apparent national differences in school belonging survive measurement and complex-sampling uncertainty?
approach: Validate the BELONG, bullying and ESCS indicators against the PISA codebook.
Use the final student weight and 80 Fay-BRR replicates for uncertainty.
Distinguish country-level descriptions from individual-level socioeconomic associations.
Evaluate scaling comparability, response quality and exclusions before interpreting rankings.
results: From 613,744 OECD PISA 2022 student rows in 80 economies, the current complete-case design-weight analysis retained 561,339 BELONG observations across 78 economies; ISR and KSV had too few complete observations for a published estimate.

Preliminary design-weighted BELONG means (95% Fay-BRR intervals): Germany 0.270 [0.240, 0.300], Finland 0.101 [0.077, 0.125], Sweden 0.088 [0.059, 0.117]. These five-country displays are illustrative, not multiplicity-adjusted rankings.

All 78 country-level estimates, standard errors, exclusions, exact data SHA-256 and R scripts are documented in the research source directory. Interpretation remains exploratory pending measurement-equivalence and response-rate review.

An independent Fay-BRR design calculation reproduced the archived PISA BELONG means and standard errors from 80 replicate-weight columns for Germany (n=5,278), Finland (n=9,736) and Sweden (n=5,820) to 1e-10 precision. Measurement equivalence remains untested.
caseStudy.limitations: OECD PISA 2022 observational student-level data. 78/80 economies were estimable under current complete-case rules; results are descriptive, not causal or measurement-invariance-validated. Low-response systems must be evaluated individually before ranking or generalization.

title: Neurobehavior Inference Lab

research.context: How do working-memory load and delay relate to speed and accuracy within repeated behavioral task trials?
methods: Read BIDS behavioral events and phenotype metadata, not MRI volumes.
Validate response correctness and prespecified reaction-time windows.
Fit participant-intercept Gaussian/log-RT and binomial mixed-effects models.

results: R mixed-effects models were fitted to 80 OpenNeuro ds000030 participants' public SCAP event files (3,840 event rows; 3,740 trials with coded accuracy; 3,241 correct trials). Both model fits were nonsingular, with no reported optimizer convergence messages. Coefficient interpretation remains exploratory.
The observed execution artifacts, input hashes, package versions and restrictions are documented in the research evidence ledger. Full reproducibility and sensitivity gates are still outstanding.
Interpretation remains exploratory and no causal, diagnostic or peer-reviewed conclusion is asserted.

Re-fitting the 80-participant SCAP task model under three correct-trial RT windows gave log-RT Load coefficients +0.04270 (0.15–3.0 s), +0.04138 (0.2–2.5 s), and +0.03919 (0.3–2.0 s). Exploratory within-task associations are not clinical or imaging effects.
caseStudy.limitations: An 80-participant convenience subset of 268 available task-event files was analyzed; the full cohort, RT thresholds, nuisance effects, hierarchical dependence and group representativeness need additional review. No fMRI or diagnostic conclusions are supported.
